hello.title: Hello, OCaml!
hello.summary: Write your first OCaml program and print text with print_endline, print_string and Printf.printf.
hello.lesson.0: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. Your first instruction is `print_endline`: it prints a piece of text and then starts a new line. Text in OCaml is called a **string**, and you write it between double quotes, like `"Hello"`.
hello.lesson.2: The line starts with `let () =`. This means: run the code on the right side when the program starts. The `()` is a special value called **unit**. It means "nothing": `print_endline` prints something, but it gives back no useful value, only `()`.
hello.lesson.3: To run several instructions one after the other, put a semicolon `;` between them. You put the semicolon between two instructions, not after the last one. OCaml does not care about line breaks or indentation, but the indentation of two spaces makes the code easy to read.
hello.lesson.6: `print_string` prints text, but it does not start a new line. The next text continues on the same line. Inside a string, `\n` is a new line character, so `print_string "Hi\n"` prints `Hi` and then starts a new line.
hello.lesson.9: `Printf.printf` prints text with placeholders. `%s` is a placeholder for a string and `%d` for a whole number. After the text you write the values for the placeholders, in the same order, separated by spaces. There are no commas and no parentheses around them.
hello.lesson.11: Like `print_string`, `Printf.printf` does not add a new line by itself. End the text with `\n` when you want the next output to start on a new line.
hello.card.4: `\n` inside a string starts a new line
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints `Hi` and then starts a new line?
hello-1.explain: `print_endline` adds a new line after the text. `print_string` does not, strings need double quotes, and OCaml has no `print` function.
hello-2.explain: `print_string` does not start a new line, so `bye` follows `Good` on the same line.
hello-3.explain: The three `%d` placeholders get the values `2`, `3` and `5` in this order.
hello-4.statement: `print_string` starts a new line after the text.
hello-4.explain: Only `print_endline` adds a new line. With `print_string` you write `\n` yourself.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the program so it prints `Hello` and `World` on two lines.
hello-5.explain: `print_endline` ends the line after `Hello`. With `print_string` or `Printf.printf` you get `HelloWorld` on one line.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the program so it prints `Name: Ada`.
hello-6.explain: `"Ada"` is a string, so the placeholder is `%s`. `%d` is for whole numbers.
hello-7.prompt: Build a program that prints `Hi` on its own line.
hello-7.explain: `let () =` runs the code when the program starts, and `print_endline` needs a string in double quotes.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `1`, `2` and `3` on separate lines.
hello-8.explain: The program starts with `let () =`. The last instruction has no semicolon after it.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.0: prints text and a new line
hello-9.pairs.1: prints text without a new line
hello-9.pairs.4: a new line inside a string
hello-10.explain: A semicolon is missing between two instructions: `print_endline "Middle";`.
hello-11.explain: `%d` needs a whole number, but `"6"` is a string. Write the number without quotes: `6`.
hello-12.explain: `print_string "A"` stays on the line, `print_endline "B"` ends it, and `C` comes on the next line.
values.title: Values and types
values.summary: Give names to values with let and get to know int, float, string and bool.
values.lesson.0: `let` gives a name to a value. Here `age` is the name and `36` is the value. A name starts with a lowercase letter. After this line, you can use `age` everywhere below it in the program.
values.lesson.2: Inside a block of code, you write `let name = value in`. The word `in` means: the name exists in the code that follows. The parentheses in `(price * count)` turn the calculation into one value for the placeholder.
values.lesson.5: Every value has a **type**. Whole numbers like `3` have the type `int`, and numbers with a dot like `2.5` have the type `float`. For `int` you use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. For `float` the operators have a dot: `+.`, `-.`, `*.` and `/.`. You print a `float` with `%f`, and `%.1f` prints it with one digit after the dot. Division of two `int` values gives a whole number: `7 / 2` is `3`. The operator `mod` gives the rest of the division: `7 mod 2` is `1`.
values.lesson.7: OCaml never mixes `int` and `float` by itself. `3 + 1.5` is an error, and so is `2.0 +. 1`. Convert first: `float_of_int 3` gives `3.`, the `float` version of `3`, and `int_of_float 2.9` gives `2`.
values.lesson.9: The operator `^` joins two strings into one. To put a number into a string, convert it with `string_of_int`. `String.length` gives the number of characters in a string.
values.lesson.11: A `bool` value is either `true` or `false`. You print it with the placeholder `%b`. In the next unit you use booleans to make decisions.
values.lesson.13: A value never changes. `let x = x + 1 in` does not change `x`: it creates a new `x` that hides the old one in the code that follows.
values.card.0: `let x = 5 in ...` gives a name to a value
values-1.explain: The second `let` creates a new `x` with the value `4 * 3`, which is `12`. Then `12 - 2` is `10`.
values-2.explain: 5 fits 3 times into 17, so `17 / 5` is `3`. The rest is `17 - 15`, so `17 mod 5` is `2`.
values-3.prompt: Which expression adds two floats correctly?
values-3.explain: Floats need the operator `+.`, and both values must be floats. `2` and `1` are `int` values.
values-4.explain: `3` is an `int` and `1.5` is a `float`. OCaml does not mix them, so `+` cannot add them.
values-5.explain: `string_of_int 3` gives the string `"3"`, and `^` joins it to `"Level "`, which ends with a space.
values-6.prompt: Complete the program so it prints `7.5`.
values-6.explain: Both values are floats, so you multiply with `*.`. `2.5 *. 3.0` is `7.5`.
values-7.prompt: Complete the program so it prints `Score: 42`.
values-7.explain: `^` joins strings, so the `int` must become a string first. `string_of_int` does that.
values-8.prompt: Build a line that gives the name `total` to the sum of `a` and `b`, for the code that follows.
values-8.explain: `let ... in` gives a name to a value. `a` and `b` are `int` values, so you add them with `+`.
values-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Area: 12`.
values-9.explain: A name must exist before you use it: `height` needs `width`, and `area` needs both.
values-10.prompt: Match the value or operator with its meaning.
values-11.explain: Both values are floats here, so you multiply with `*.`: `float_of_int count *. price`.
values-12.explain: `^` only joins strings, and `age` is an `int`. Write `string_of_int age`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions, call them with arguments, and use functions without a name.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** turns input values into a result. `let square x = x * x` defines a function with the name `square` and one **parameter**, `x`. The code after `=` is the body. Its value is the result, so OCaml needs no `return`.
functions.lesson.2: To call a function, write its name and then the argument, separated by a space: `square 5`. You need parentheses only to group things. A call comes before the other operators, so `square 2 + 3` means `(square 2) + 3`.
functions.lesson.5: A function can have several parameters, separated by spaces. When you call it, you also separate the arguments with spaces, without commas.
functions.lesson.7: OCaml finds the types of a function by itself. The type of `area` is `int -> int -> int`: it takes two `int` values and gives an `int`. The arrow `->` separates the inputs from the result. The type of `greet` is `string -> string`.
functions.lesson.9: `fun x -> x * 2` is a function without a name. It takes `x` and gives `x * 2`. You can give it a name with `let`. `let double = fun x -> x * 2` is the same as `let double x = x * 2`.
functions.lesson.11: When you give a function only its first argument, you get a new function that waits for the rest. This is called **partial application**. Here `add 10` is a function that adds `10` to its argument.
functions.lesson.13: A function that needs no input takes `()` as its parameter: `let say_hi () = print_endline "Hi"`. You call it with `say_hi ()`.
functions.card.0: `let square x = x * x` defines a function
functions.card.2: `let area w h = w * h` has the type `int -> int -> int`
functions.card.3: `fun x -> x + 1` is a function without a name
functions.card.4: `let add_ten = add 10` gives only the first argument
functions-1.explain: `triple 4` runs the body with `x = 4`, so the result is `4 * 3`.
functions-2.explain: The call comes first: `double 3 + 1` means `(double 3) + 1`, which is `6 + 1`.
functions-3.prompt: The function is `let area w h = w * h`. How do you call it with `3` and `4`?
functions-3.explain: You separate the arguments with spaces. With commas, `3, 4` becomes one value with two parts.
functions-4.explain: `add 5` is a new function that waits for the second argument. `add_five 10` is `5 + 10`.
functions-5.statement: These two lines define the same function.
functions-5.explain: `let inc x = ...` is a short way to write `let inc = fun x -> ...`. Both take `x` and give `x + 1`.
functions-6.prompt: Complete the function so the program prints `Hi, Ada`.
functions-6.explain: `^` joins two strings. `+` and `+.` work only with numbers.
functions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `8`.
functions-7.explain: A function without a name starts with `fun`, then the parameter, `->` and the body.
functions-8.prompt: Build a function `area` that multiplies its two parameters `w` and `h`.
functions-8.explain: The parameters follow the name, separated by spaces. The body after `=` is the result, without `return`.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hello, Ada!`.
functions-9.explain: You define `greet` first. Only then can the code below it call `greet "Ada"`.
functions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
functions-10.pairs.3: the type of a function from int to int
functions-11.explain: Arguments are separated by spaces, not commas: `(add 2 3)`.
functions-12.prompt: The program should print `Hi` and then `Bye`. Which line has the bug?
functions-12.explain: `say_hi` alone only names the function. To call it, give it the argument `()`: `say_hi ();`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Choose between values with if, then and else, compare values, and match a value against patterns.
conditions.lesson.0: `if condition then a else b` gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` when it is `false`. In OCaml, `if` is an **expression**: it has a value, like `2 + 3` has a value. Both branches must have the same type.
conditions.lesson.2: You compare values with `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. The result is a `bool`. You combine conditions with `&&` (and) and `||` (or), and `not` turns `true` into `false` and back.
conditions.lesson.4: For more than two choices, put another `if` after `else`. OCaml checks the conditions from top to bottom and uses the first one that is `true`.
conditions.lesson.6: You can leave out `else` only when the `then` branch gives `()`, for example when it prints: `if n > 0 then print_endline "positive"`. In all other cases, `else` is required.
conditions.lesson.8: `match x with` compares a value with **patterns**, one after the other. Each case starts with `|`, then the pattern, `->` and the result. The first pattern that fits wins. The pattern `_` fits every value, so it usually comes last.
conditions.lesson.10: One case can have several patterns, separated by `|`. You can match strings, numbers, booleans and more.
conditions.lesson.12: OCaml also has `==` and `!=`, but they check something else. To compare two values, always use `=` and `<>`.
conditions.card.0: `if x > 0 then "pos" else "neg"` has a value
conditions-1.explain: 8 is not greater than 10, but it is greater than 5, so the second branch gives `medium`.
conditions-2.explain: `2` does not fit `0`, but it fits one of the patterns `1 | 2 | 3`.
conditions-3.prompt: Which operator means "not equal" in OCaml?
conditions-3.explain: `a <> b` is `true` when `a` and `b` are different. The other operators do not exist in OCaml.
conditions-4.explain: `a > 5` is `false`, but `b > 5` is `true`. With `||`, one `true` condition is enough.
conditions-5.explain: Both branches of an `if` must have the same type. `"big"` is a string, but `0` is an `int`.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `even`.
conditions-6.explain: `10 mod 2` is `0`, and `=` checks that two values are equal, so the condition is `true`.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the last case so the program prints `weekday`.
conditions-7.explain: Every case starts with `|`, and `_` is the pattern that fits every other value.
conditions-8.prompt: Build an expression that gives `"yes"` when `x` is greater than `0`, and `"no"` otherwise.
conditions-8.explain: `if condition then a else b` is an expression. The `then` branch is used when the condition is `true`.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `B`.
conditions-9.explain: The function starts with `if`. Each `else` follows the branch before it, and the last line calls the function.
conditions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
conditions-10.pairs.3: at least one must be true
conditions-10.pairs.4: a pattern that fits every value
conditions-11.explain: All cases must give the same type. The other cases give strings, so the last one needs a string too, for example `| _ -> "many"`.
conditions-12.explain: OCaml writes "and" in a condition as `&&`: `if age >= 18 && age < 65 then`.
lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Store many values in a list, add and join lists, and work with every element using List functions.
lists.lesson.0: A **list** holds several values of the same type, in order. You write it in square brackets and separate the elements with semicolons: `[1; 2; 3]`. `[]` is the empty list. A list of `int` values has the type `int list`.
lists.lesson.1: The operator `::` puts one element in front of a list: `0 :: [1; 2]` is `[0; 1; 2]`. The operator `@` joins two lists. `List.length` gives the number of elements. Like all values, a list never changes: `::` and `@` create new lists.
lists.lesson.4: `List.iter f list` calls the function `f` with every element, from first to last. It is useful for printing.
lists.lesson.6: `List.map f list` calls `f` with every element and collects the results in a new list. A function without a name is handy here.
lists.lesson.8: `List.filter f list` keeps only the elements for which `f` gives `true`. The order of the elements stays the same.
lists.lesson.10: `String.concat sep list` joins a list of strings into one string, with `sep` between the elements. Together with `List.map` and `string_of_int`, it prints a list of numbers on one line.
lists.lesson.12: Use semicolons in lists, not commas. `[1, 2, 3]` is not a list of three numbers: it is a list with only one element, the group `1, 2, 3`.
lists.card.0: `[1; 2; 3]` is a list, `[]` the empty list
lists.card.1: `0 :: nums` adds in front, `a @ b` joins
lists-1.explain: `b` is `[0; 1; 2; 3]`: `0` in front, then `a`, then `3`. That is 4 elements.
lists-2.explain: `List.map` multiplies every element by itself: 1, 4, 9 and 16.
lists-3.prompt: Which one is a list of three numbers?
lists-3.explain: Lists use square brackets and semicolons. `[1, 2, 3]` is a list with one element.
lists-4.explain: Only `4` and `2` are less than `5`. `List.filter` keeps them in their original order.
lists-5.statement: `List.map` gives a new list and leaves the original list unchanged.
lists-5.explain: Lists never change. `List.map` builds a new list with the results.
lists-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `a`, `b` and `c` on separate lines.
lists-6.explain: `List.iter` calls `print_endline` with every element. `List.map` would build a new list instead.
lists-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `3`.
lists-7.explain: `hi`, `hello` and `hey` have fewer than 6 characters, so `<` keeps 3 words.
lists-8.prompt: Build a line that puts `0` in front of `nums` and names the result `all`.
lists-8.explain: `::` puts one element in front of a list. `@` joins two lists, so it needs `[0]`.
lists-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `20` and `40`.
lists-9.explain: First keep the even numbers `2` and `4`, then multiply them by 10, then print them.
lists-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
lists-10.pairs.1: puts x in front of xs
lists-10.pairs.4: keeps the elements that pass a test
lists-11.explain: The elements of a list are separated by semicolons: `[3; 6; 9]`.
lists-12.explain: `@` joins two lists, but `"Cy"` is a string. Put it in a list: `names @ ["Cy"]`.
recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.summary: Write functions that call themselves with let rec, take lists apart with patterns, and use accumulators.
recursion.lesson.0: A **recursive** function calls itself. In OCaml you define it with `let rec` instead of `let`. Without `rec`, the function cannot see its own name, and you get an error.
recursion.lesson.2: `factorial 5` is `5 * factorial 4`, and `factorial 4` is `4 * factorial 3`, and so on. When `n` reaches `1`, the function stops calling itself and gives `1`. This stopping point is the **base case**. The result is `5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1`, which is `120`.
recursion.lesson.4: Every list is either empty, `[]`, or a first element followed by the rest of the list, `head :: tail`. With `match` you handle both patterns. In the second case, the names `head` and `tail` get the first element and the rest.
recursion.lesson.6: `sum [3; 5; 7]` is `3 + sum [5; 7]`, then `3 + 5 + sum [7]`, then `3 + 5 + 7 + sum []`. The empty list is the base case and gives `0`. In the same way, a recursive function can build a new list with `::`.
recursion.lesson.9: An **accumulator** is an extra parameter that carries the result so far. Here the helper function `go` is defined inside `sum`. It adds each element to `acc`, and at the end of the list it gives `acc`. The call `go 0 list` starts with `0`. Because the recursive call is the last step, this version also works with very long lists.
recursion.lesson.11: When you do not need a value from a pattern, write `_` instead of a name: `| _ :: rest -> 1 + count rest` counts the elements without looking at them.
recursion.lesson.12: Every recursive function needs a base case, and each call must come closer to it. Otherwise the function calls itself again and again until the program crashes.
recursion.card.0: `let rec f n = ... f (n - 1) ...` calls itself
recursion.card.1: a base case stops the recursion
recursion.card.3: `let rec go acc xs = ...` carries the result in `acc`
recursion-2.explain: Each element adds `1`, and the empty list adds `0`. The list has 3 elements.
recursion-3.explain: The result is `2 * 3 * 4 * 1`, which is `24`. The base case gives `1`, so it does not change the product.
recursion-4.explain: The function calls itself, so it needs `let rec power2 n =`. With only `let`, the name `power2` is unknown inside the body.
recursion-5.prompt: In the pattern `x :: rest`, what is `rest`?
recursion-5.options.0: The list without its first element
recursion-5.options.1: The last element of the list
recursion-5.options.2: The first element of the list
recursion-5.explain: `x` is the first element and `rest` is the list of all the other elements.
recursion-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `6`.
recursion-6.explain: `sum` calls itself, so it must be defined with `let rec`.
recursion-7.prompt: Complete the base case so the program prints `24`.
recursion-7.explain: The empty list must give `1`, because multiplying by `1` changes nothing. With `0`, the whole product would be `0`.
recursion-8.prompt: Build the first line of the helper `go`. It takes the accumulator `acc` first and then the list `rest`.
recursion-8.explain: `go` calls itself, so it needs `let rec`. The parameters follow the name, separated by spaces.
recursion-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `24`.
recursion-9.explain: The function comes first, with the base case in the `if` branch. The program then calls `factorial 4`, which is `4 * 3 * 2 * 1`.
recursion-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
recursion-10.pairs.0: defines a function that can call itself
recursion-10.pairs.1: the pattern for the empty list
recursion-10.pairs.2: the pattern for a first element and the rest
recursion-10.pairs.3: a pattern for a value you do not need
recursion-10.pairs.4: calls go with a new accumulator
recursion-11.explain: `rest` is a list, not a number. The function must call itself on the rest: `x + sum rest`.
recursion-12.prompt: The function should count the numbers greater than 10. Which line has the bug?
recursion-12.explain: Before counting anything, the count is zero, so the accumulator must start at `0`: `go 0 list`.
types.title: Variants and records
types.summary: Define your own types: variants for values with several cases, and records for values with named fields.
types.lesson.0: With `type` you define your own type. A **variant** type lists all possible cases. Each case is a **constructor** and starts with an uppercase letter. A value of type `color` is always `Red`, `Green` or `Blue`, nothing else.
types.lesson.2: `match` and variants work well together. If you forget a case, the compiler warns you. So when you add a new case to a type, OCaml shows you every `match` that must handle it.
types.lesson.3: A constructor can carry data. You write the type of the data after `of`. In `Rect of float * float`, the `*` means "and": a `Rect` carries two floats. You create it with a pair in parentheses, `Rect (2.0, 3.0)`, and the pattern `Rect (w, h)` takes the pair apart.
types.lesson.6: A **record** groups several values, each with a name. These named parts are called **fields**. In the type, each field has a name and a type: `{ name : string; age : int }`. You create a record with `=` for each field, and you read a field with a dot: `p.name`.
types.lesson.8: A record never changes. `{ p with age = 37 }` creates a copy of `p` in which only `age` is different. The original record stays the same.
types.lesson.10: Records can also be patterns. `{ x = 0; y = 0 }` fits only that exact point. In `{ x = 0; _ }`, the `_` means that the other fields can have any value.
types.lesson.12: Constructors like `Circle` start with an uppercase letter. Type names, field names and other names like `shape`, `age` and `area` start with a lowercase letter.
types.card.1: `type shape = Circle of float | Rect of float * float`
types.card.3: `p.name` reads a field, `{ p with age = 37 }` copies
types.card.4: `match s with | Circle r -> ... | Rect (w, h) -> ...`
types-1.explain: The value is `Yellow`, so the case `Yellow -> "wait"` fits.
types-2.explain: `q` is a copy of `p` with a new `name`. The `age` stays `30`.
types-3.explain: `Rect (2, 5)` has the area `10` and `Square 3` has the area `9`. Together that is `19`.
types-4.statement: A constructor can start with a lowercase letter, like `red`.
types-4.explain: Constructors always start with an uppercase letter, like `Red`. Lowercase names are for values, functions, types and fields.
types-5.prompt: The type is `type person = { name : string; age : int }`. Which code creates a `person`?
types-5.explain: Each field gets its value with `=`, and the fields are separated by semicolons.
types-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Ada`.
types-6.explain: You read a field of a record with a dot: `p.name`.
types-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `5.0`.
types-7.explain: A `Rect` carries a pair, so its values go in parentheses with a comma. `2.0 *. 2.5` is `5.0`.
types-8.prompt: Build a copy of the record `p` in which `age` is `37`.
types-8.explain: `{ p with age = 37 }` copies all fields of `p` and changes only `age`.
types-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ada 37`.
types-9.explain: The type comes first. Then you create `p`, make the copy `q` from it, and print `q`.
types-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
types-10.pairs.2: a case that carries a float
types-10.pairs.4: a copy with one field changed
types-11.explain: `side` is a float, so you multiply with `*.`: `side *. side`.
types-12.explain: A new record needs a value for every field. Add the age: `{ name = "Ada"; age = 36 }`.
options.title: Options and more patterns
options.summary: Handle missing values with option, add conditions to patterns with when, and combine lists with List.fold_left.
options.lesson.0: Sometimes there is no result, for example when you divide by zero. For this, OCaml has the type `option`. An option is either `Some x`, which holds a value `x`, or `None`, which holds nothing. `Some 5` has the type `int option`.
options.lesson.2: The standard library uses options too. `List.find_opt f list` gives `Some x` with the first element for which `f` gives `true`, or `None` when there is no such element.
options.lesson.4: An `int option` is not an `int`. `Some 5 + 1` is an error. You must first use `match` to handle both cases. This way, you can never forget the case where the value is missing.
options.lesson.6: `when` adds a condition to a pattern. The case fits only when the pattern fits and the condition is `true`. In `| x when x < 0`, the name `x` gets the value, and the condition checks it.
options.lesson.9: `List.fold_left f start list` combines all elements of a list into one value. The function `f` gets the result so far, called the accumulator, and the next element, and gives the new result. It works like the accumulator from the recursion unit, but you do not write the recursion yourself.
options.lesson.11: For `total`, the accumulator starts at `0` and becomes `1`, `3`, `6` and finally `10`. The start value and the result can also be strings or lists.
options.lesson.13: An operator in parentheses is a function: `( + )` takes two numbers and adds them. So `List.fold_left ( + ) 0 nums` also gives the sum of `nums`.
